introduction-why-culture-eats-strategy-f.core: Culture (how people actually behave, share information and treat failure) determines whether a strategy can be executed. In engineering it shows in information flow, psychological safety and how incidents are handled.

first_principles.problem: A great strategy fails because people hide problems, don't speak up, and blame each other.
truths: Information flow determines how fast problems surface.

analogy.title: Soil for plants
analogy.story: The best seeds (strategy) fail in poor soil (culture).
analogy.breaks: Culture is shaped slowly by consistent leadership behaviour, not by posters.

example.title: Same strategy, two cultures
flow: Culture A: bad news hidden → late failures
Culture B: problems raised early → fixed cheaply
example.outcome: culture treated as an engineering concern.

check.q: Why does culture matter so much to engineering performance?
check.a: It determines whether problems surface early, people collaborate and failures are learned from.

psychological-safety-the-foundation-of-h.core: Google's Project Aristotle found psychological safety (the belief that you can take interpersonal risks like asking questions, admitting mistakes or disagreeing without punishment) was the top predictor of team effectiveness.

first_principles.problem: Junior engineers don't ask questions, and seniors don't admit mistakes, so problems stay hidden until they explode.
derivation: **Model fallibility** ('I might be wrong', 'I made a mistake').
**Respond to bad news with curiosity**, not anger.
**Invite input** explicitly, especially from quieter members.

analogy.title: A classroom where wrong answers are welcome
analogy.story: Students learn faster when they aren't afraid to answer incorrectly.
analogy.breaks: Safety isn't comfort. High standards and candid feedback still apply.

example.title: A leader's reaction to a mistake
flow: 'Who did this?!' → team hides next issue
'Thanks for flagging fast. What can we learn?' → issues surface early

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One reaction sets the norm for months.

check.q: What did Google's Project Aristotle identify as the top factor in team effectiveness?

westrums-organizational-typology-how-inf.core: Westrum classified organisational cultures by how they handle information. Pathological (power-oriented: messengers shot, information hoarded), bureaucratic (rule-oriented: messengers ignored, narrow responsibilities) and generative (performance-oriented: messengers trained, information flows, failures lead to inquiry).

first_principles.problem: In power-oriented cultures, bad news never reaches decision makers until it's too late.
truths: How information flows shapes safety and performance.
DORA links generative culture to delivery performance.
Culture type can be measured with surveys.
derivation: **Bureaucratic**: rules, silos, a 'not my job' attitude.
**Measure** with Westrum survey questions and improve.

analogy.title: Three hospitals handling a nurse's warning
analogy.story: One punishes the nurse, one files the report in a drawer, one investigates and fixes the cause.
analogy.breaks: Organisations are mixtures. Different teams can sit at different points.

example.title: Survey statements (DORA-style)
example.outcome: information flow treated as a cultural KPI.

check.q: How does a generative culture treat messengers who bring bad news?
check.a: It trains and values them, using the information to improve.

just-culture-accountability-without-blam.core: Just culture distinguishes human error (console the person, fix the system), at-risk behaviour (coach, and remove the incentives for shortcuts) and reckless behaviour (sanction). Accountability means learning and repair, not automatic punishment.

first_principles.problem: The 'bad apple' theory fires people after outages, so others hide mistakes and the systemic causes remain.
truths: Most errors come from system conditions.
derivation: **Human error** → support the person, fix the design.
**At-risk behaviour** (normalised shortcuts) → coaching, fix the incentives.
**Forward-looking accountability**: own the fix and the learning.

analogy.title: Traffic justice
analogy.story: An honest mistake at a confusing junction leads to fixing the signs; drink-driving leads to prosecution.
analogy.breaks: Defining 'reckless' needs care, and hindsight makes everything look reckless.

example.title: Classifying a production change mistake
flow: Engineer skipped staging (team habit under deadline)
Response: coaching + make staging fast + enforce in pipeline

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fairness kept, and the shortcut removed systemically.

example.outcome: accountability that improves systems and keeps trust.

check.q: How does just culture respond to at-risk behaviour?
check.a: With coaching and by removing the incentives or conditions that made the shortcut attractive.

the-blameless-post-mortem-just-culture-i.core: Blameless postmortems put just culture into operation: focus on how the system allowed the failure, reconstruct the decisions people made with the information they had, and produce systemic actions, so people report fully and honestly.

first_principles.problem: Postmortems turn into blame sessions, and future incidents are reported vaguely or covered up.
derivation: Reconstruct the **local rationality**: why did it make sense then?

analogy.title: A flight data recorder review
analogy.story: Investigators reconstruct what the pilots saw and why their actions made sense, then fix cockpit design.
analogy.breaks: 'Blameless' still allows discussing actions candidly. It isn't a ban on naming what happened.

example.title: A facilitation script

code.text:
"We assume everyone acted with good intent and the best information available.
Our goal is to understand how our system allowed this, not to find fault.
Walk us through what you saw and why it made sense at that moment."

example.outcome: postmortems that teach rather than punish.

check.q: What is 'local rationality' in a blameless postmortem?
check.a: Understanding why a person's actions made sense given what they knew and saw at the time.

the-learning-organization-putting-it-all.core: A learning organisation continuously improves through experience. Psychological safety lets problems surface, generative information flow spreads them, just culture and blameless reviews turn them into system changes, and leaders model curiosity.

first_principles.problem: Organisations repeat mistakes because lessons stay local or never get acted on.
truths: Lessons must be shared beyond one team.
derivation: **Leaders model** learning; **measure** with surveys and repeat-incident rates.

analogy.title: A scientific community
analogy.story: Experiments, honest reporting of failures, peer review and building on each other's findings.
analogy.breaks: Learning takes time and slack, and fully utilised teams can't learn.

example.title: Org-wide learning rituals
flow: Monthly incident review open to all
example.outcome: an organisation that gets better every year.

check.q: What prevents an organisation from learning even when teams run postmortems?
check.a: Lessons staying local: not shared widely, or actions not followed through.
